L156: Questions What is the history of the marquise cut? + The marquise cut was commissioned in 1740 by King Louis XV of France, who asked his jewelers to design a diamond that mirrored the smile of his mistress, the Marquise de Pompadour. The result was an elongated oval with two sharp points, originally called the navette (little boat). It is one of the oldest named diamond shapes still in regular use and carries one of the most romantic origin stories in fine jewelry.
L157: Will the points of the marquise chip? + The two points of a marquise are the most vulnerable part of the stone. Our setting uses V-tip prongs, a tip shaped specifically to cover and shield each point from impact. This is the industry standard protective setting for marquise and pear cuts. Treat the ring as fine jewelry, avoid sleeping or showering in it, and the points will last generations. Lifetime warranty covers stone repair from manufacturing defect.
L158: Why is marquise considered an old soul cut? + Marquise peaked in popularity during the Edwardian, Art Deco, and 1970s eras. It is associated with vintage estate jewelry, heirloom rings, and the era of long elegant hands. Modern engagement ring shopping skews heavily toward round and oval. Choosing marquise reads as deliberate, as preferring the language of an older era over a current trend. The cut signals taste shaped by reading and looking, not by social feeds.
L159: Is 3 carats too big for a marquise? + A 3 carat marquise is 14.10mm long, which is the visual length of approximately a 4.5 carat round. Marquise wears larger than its actual carat weight because the eye traces the long axis of the stone. On most hands the 3 carat reads as substantial without becoming impractical. If you are between sizes, marquise is the cut where length flatters the finger most. We recommend asking for a free print at home sizer at info@dracodiamond.com.
L160: Which metal should I choose? + Yellow gold reads the most historically accurate, marquise cuts were almost always set in yellow gold during their Edwardian and Louis XV peaks. White gold and platinum give a cleaner modern read and let the diamond do the work. Rose gold sits romantic and pairs well with the vintage shape. Platinum is the most durable for daily wear and recommended for engagement use. Silver delivers the white gold effect at the lowest price point.

L152: Questions What is an asscher cut? + Asscher is a square step cut with octagonal corners, developed in 1902 by Joseph Asscher in the Netherlands. It uses parallel rectangular facets that produce the famous hall of mirrors effect, infinite reflections looking into the stone. Unlike brilliant cuts which scatter light into sparkle, asscher organizes light into long flashes. It became the defining cut of the Art Deco era and is associated with Elizabeth Taylor's famous 33-carat Krupp diamond.
L153: Why does grade matter more on an asscher? + Asscher's step cut acts like a window into the stone. The wide parallel facets show inclusions and color tint far more visibly than the busy faceting of a round brilliant. A G or H color round looks bright. A G or H color asscher looks visibly warm. The same applies to clarity. This is why we hold E to F color and VS plus clarity on every asscher, even though the cost is higher. On this cut, you see what you paid for.
L154: Are lab grown diamonds real diamonds? + They are diamonds. Lab grown diamonds are chemically, physically, and optically identical to mined diamonds. A gemologist cannot tell the difference without specialized equipment. In 2018 the FTC removed the word natural from its definition of a diamond. IGI grades them on the same cut, color, clarity, and carat scale as mined stones. The only difference is origin.
L155: What are guardian backs? + Guardian backs are a secure earring closure with a flat backing disc that prevents the earring from sliding forward off the post. Combined with the screw or threaded post, they hold heavy stud earrings in place far better than standard friction backs. Standard on every Draco stud over 1 carat per ear. Which metal should I choose? + White gold and platinum let the asscher's geometry do the work, the cleanest, most architectural look.
